habitat: Silver-haired bats range across most of North America, from southern Canada throughout the United States to northeastern Mexico. They are highly migratory in the northern parts of their range, traveling south for winter. During summer, they roost in tree cavities, under loose bark, in woodpecker holes, and occasionally in buildings. They prefer mature, old-growth forests near water sources. During migration, they may appear in unexpected urban locations, stopping to rest on buildings, fences, and even ships at sea.
diet: Silver-haired bats are insectivores, feeding primarily on moths, flies, beetles, caddisflies, and other flying insects. They are slow, deliberate flyers compared to other bats, typically hunting along forest edges, over water, and in woodland clearings 5-15 meters above ground. They use echolocation to detect prey, emitting frequency-modulated calls at 30-40 kHz. Like all bats, they provide enormous ecological benefits by consuming crop pests and disease-carrying insects — a single bat may eat over 1,000 insects in one night.
behavior: Silver-haired bats are solitary for much of the year, roosting alone or in small maternity colonies of 5-25 females during summer. They emerge to hunt approximately 30-60 minutes after sunset, later than many other bat species — contributing to their relative obscurity. Males and females typically roost separately during summer. They are one of the slowest-flying bats in North America (about 17-18 km/h), with a distinctive fluttering flight pattern. During fall migration, they may be found in mixed-species flocks with red bats and hoary bats.
facts: The silver-haired bat gets its name from the silvery-white tips on its otherwise black or dark brown fur, giving it a frosted, silver appearance. It is one of the most common bat species struck by wind turbines, particularly during fall migration — a significant conservation concern. They have a relatively long lifespan for a small mammal, living up to 12 years in the wild. Unlike many bats, they do not hibernate in caves, instead relying on tree cavities and buildings for winter shelter.
naming: Silver-haired bat names might reflect their distinctive frosted coloring, nocturnal nature, or flight. Consider names like Silver, Frost, Luna, Dusk, Storm, Whisper, Glimmer, Echo, Shade, Mist, Shadow, Argent (Latin for silver), Vesper (evening), or Cirrus (wispy, like their fur tips).
